newsitem.title: ITALY: Case of convicted leftists grips Italy.
newsitem.headline: Case of convicted leftists grips Italy.

text.p: One of Italy's most celebrated left-wing thinkers was jailed on Friday for the murder of a policeman in 1972 after a guilty verdict that has caused a furore in corridors of power occupied by some of his admirers.

Adriano Sofri, who had been a leader of the now defunct revolutionary group Lotta Continua, was picked up by police at his home near Florence and taken to Pisa jail to serve 19 years, nine months and eight days for murder.
"They've come to take me. Thank you very much and all the best," Sofri told reporters outside his home.

The arrest was carried out after Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, rejected any further appeal by Sofri and co-defendants Ovidio Bompressi and Giorgio Pietrostefani against their convictions.

The three, who have protested their innocence, were sentenced to 22 years in jail, reduced by the amount of time they have spent in detention since they were charged in 1988 for the shooting of police detective Luigi Calabresi in May 1972.

Bompressi announced through his lawyer on Friday that he was ready to turn himself in. Pietrostefani told a television interviewer from Paris, where he has lived for five years, that he intended to return home to surrender.
Critics of the convictions slammed the time the case has taken as symbol of a sick justice system.

"I hope that it won't be too long before we live in a country where it does not take 22 years to clear up how a tragedy like the killing of Commissioner Calabresi happened," said deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni, who knows Sofri.

Magistrates, journalists and other supporters of the three have questioned how the judges managed to convict them on what they say is the evidence of a single turncoat and have made clear they intend to campaign for a state pardon.
Lotta Continua -- Continuous Struggle -- was a movement of revolutionary intellectuals in the turbulent 1970s, when Italy was gripped by violence from the extreme left and right.
The movement inspired many leftists, several of whom now hold senior positions in government, the media and the law.
Calabresi was a hated figure to young leftists who blamed him for the death of an anarchist being questioned about a bomb attack in 1969 which killed 16 people at a bank in Milan.

The anarchist, Giuseppe Pinelli, was officially said to have jumped from a window of Milan police headquarters. His fate inspired the play "Accidental Death of an Anarchist" by Italian playwright Dario Fo.
Lotta Continua's newspaper ran a gleeful headline the day after Calabresi was shot outside his home.

But Sofri and the others were not implicated until 1988 when a witness, Leonardo Marino, walked into a police station in 1988 and said he and the three others were behind Calabresi's death. Marino has already been sentenced to 11 years in jail.
A first trial found Sofri, Bompressi and Pietrostefani guilty in 1990. They were acquitted on appeal in 1993 only for the Court of Cassation to order a retrial in 1994.

Sofri, who is in his 50s, has said the sentence is the equivalent of life in prison. But he and the others say they do not intend to seek a pardon from President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro because it would be tantamount to a false admission of guilt.
